meta.title: The metric description of viscoelasticity and instabilities in viscoelastic solids
meta.abstractHtml:
Many manmade and naturally occurring materials form viscoelastic solids. The increasing use of biologically inspired elastomeric material and the extreme mechanical response these elastomers offer drive the need for a better, more intuitive and quantitative understanding of the mechanical response of such continua. This is in particular important in determining the stability of viscoelastic structure over time where in lieu of robust rules we often must resort to simulations.

In this work we put forward a metric description of viscoelasticity in which the continua is characterized by temporally evolving reference lengths quantified by a rest reference metric. This rest reference metric serves as a state variable describing the result of the viscoelastic flow in the system, and allows us to provide robust claims regarding stability of incompressible isotropic viscoelastic media. We demonstrate these claims for a simple bistable systems of three standard-linear-solid spring dashpot assemblies where the predicted rules can be verified by explicit calculations, and also show quantitative agreement with recent experiments in viscoelastic silicone rubber shells that display delayed stability loss.

children.title: Abstract
children.body:
Many manmade and naturally occurring materials form viscoelastic solids. The increasing use of biologically inspired elastomeric material and the extreme mechanical response these elastomers offer drive the need for a better, more intuitive and quantitative understanding of the mechanical response of such continua. This is in particular important in determining the stability of viscoelastic structure over time where in lieu of robust rules we often must resort to simulations.

In this work we put forward a metric description of viscoelasticity in which the continua is characterized by temporally evolving reference lengths quantified by a rest reference metric. This rest reference metric serves as a state variable describing the result of the viscoelastic flow in the system, and allows us to provide robust claims regarding stability of incompressible isotropic viscoelastic media. We demonstrate these claims for a simple bistable systems of three standard-linear-solid spring dashpot assemblies where the predicted rules can be verified by explicit calculations, and also show quantitative agreement with recent experiments in viscoelastic silicone rubber shells that display delayed stability loss.

Elastomeric solids are ubiquitous materials composed of cross-linked long molecular chains and display extreme mechanical response properties. Examples include latex rubber, silicone rubbers Treloar (1975) as well as the crosslinked proteins resilin and elastin responsible for the mechanical properties of tissues such as ligaments and arteries Andersen (1963); Neuman and Logan (1950); Gosline et al. (2002). Elastomeric solids are characterized by low elastic moduli, and reversible deformations even at strains exceeding one hundred percent. However, they also show stress relaxation when held at constant displacement and creep under a constant load Christensen (2012). These creep and stress relaxation phenomena are dissipative yet are reversible. Unlike viscoelastic fluids, elastomeric solids retain the topology of material elements in the body indefinitely. Moreover, they display only fractional stress relaxation, supporting a finite fraction of the stress even after arbitrarily long relaxation times.

gist.html: Elastomers creep and relax stress reversibly, yet keep their topology and a finite fraction of stress indefinitely.

children.title: Spring–dashpot models of creep and stress relaxation
children.body: A dashpot is a piston in a viscous fluid: its force is proportional to its rate of extension, $F=\eta\dot x$, while a spring's force is proportional to its extension, $F=kx$. Combining the two gives the simplest models of viscoelasticity. In the Maxwell model a spring and a dashpot sit in series: held at fixed extension, the force decays exponentially to zero with time $\eta/k$ (stress relaxation), and under constant load it extends without limit, as a fluid flows. In the Kelvin–Voigt model they sit in parallel: under constant load the extension approaches its final value gradually (creep), but a sudden stretch meets infinite resistance. The standard linear solid adds a spring in parallel to a Maxwell element: it responds at once like a spring, relaxes only part of the force, and creeps to a finite extension, as cross-linked elastomers do. The fraction of force it relaxes is the paper's $\beta$.

One of the most fascinating phenomena displayed by elastomeric materials is delayed stability loss, in which a fast instability releasing the elastically stored energy in a system is preceded by a slow creep. Such phenomena have been observed in the rapid snapping of the Venus fly-trap leaf  Forterre et al. (2005) activated by the plant to capture prey, in the passive snap through of thin elastomeric shells known as jumping poppers  Pandey et al. (2014); Urbach and Efrati (2018), and for non-elastomeric materials in the slow crustal dynamics leading to some earthquakes Freed and Lin (2001); Reches et al. (1994).

gist.html: In delayed stability loss a slow creep precedes a fast snap: Venus fly-traps, jumping poppers, some earthquakes.

children.body: The equations of state for viscoelastic materials commonly relate the stress to the full history of the strain in the body through a material dependent memory kernel Christensen (2012). Such equations of state accurately capture the material response, and may be used to numerically study the response of viscoelastic structures given their geometry and loading conditions Santer (2010); Brinkmeyer et al. (2012). However, they rarely allow explicit solutions and provide very little insight to the state of the viscoelastic material and its general response properties. The lack of intuition for viscoelastic dynamics is exceptionally evident when considering viscoelastic instabilities; as linear stress relaxation acts to reduce local stresses it is expected to have a stabilizing effect and in particular never cause a meta-stable state to lose stability. More elaborated variations of this hand waving argument, as we show in section IV B, only prove it stronger rather than refute it, thus elucidating the subtle nature of viscoelastic instabilities.

gist.html: Memory-kernel laws simulate well but explain little; relaxation seems bound to stabilize, which makes viscoelastic instabilities puzzling.

children.title: Hereditary integrals and the memory kernel
children.body: Linear viscoelasticity rests on Boltzmann's superposition principle: the stress now is the sum of the responses to all past strain increments, each weighted by how long ago it happened. For one strain component, $\sigma(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}G(t-s)\,\dot\varepsilon(s)\,ds$, where the relaxation function $G$ starts at the instantaneous modulus and decays to the equilibrium modulus of a solid, or to zero for a fluid. Equivalently, the stress is an elastic term plus an integral of the past strain against a memory kernel, the derivative of $G$. Such laws fit measured creep and relaxation curves and can be used in numerical simulations, but they leave the state of the material implicit: to know its present response one needs its whole history. For questions of stability the paper replaces that history by one evolving geometric object, the reference length or reference metric.

In this works we describe a metric approach to viscoelasticity and viscoelastic stability. We begin by describing one dimensional viscoelastic systems through temporally evolving rest lengths and specifically formulate the dynamics of the standard linear solid (SLS) model as a spring with temporally evolving rest length. We then consider an assembly of three SLS springs in the form of a Von-Misses truss as a first example of transient elastic stability in viscoelastic systems. We conclude the section describing this one dimensional motion by using the temporally evolving rest lengths to prove general claims regarding the elastic stability and stationarity of a general 1D, SLS systems.

gist.html: Plan of the one-dimensional part: the standard linear solid as an evolving spring, a truss, general 1D claims.

children.body: The intuitive results we obtain for one dimensional SLS systems can be generalized to full three dimensional systems. We next do so by constructing a covariant metric description of viscoelastic solids. The theory describes the material response as elastic with respect to a time dependent three dimensional reference metric. We elucidate the notions of quasi static approximation, transient elastic stability and isotropicity in light of this new description. We then discuss results regarding the quasi-static dynamics when considering isotropic and incompressible materials. Several claims regarding the elastic stability and stationary states of such bodies are shown.

gist.html: Plan of the continuum part: a covariant metric description, then claims for isotropic incompressible bodies.
Rewriting viscoelasticity as elasticity about evolving reference lengths turns the stability of creeping solids into simple rules.

brief.html: Elastomers creep and relax stress, yet keep part of their stress indefinitely, and some creep slowly before snapping, as Venus fly-traps and jumping poppers do. Constitutive laws with a memory kernel simulate such behaviour but give little insight, and the naive view that relaxation only stabilizes leaves the snapping unexplained. The paper rewrites viscoelasticity as elasticity about evolving rest lengths, first for springs in one dimension, then as a metric theory of continua, and derives stability rules from it.

A standard linear solid is a spring of fixed stiffness whose reference length relaxes towards its current and rest lengths.

brief.html: The standard linear solid is a spring of stiffness $(1-\beta)k$ in parallel with a spring $\beta k$ and a dashpot in series. Grouping its lengths into one reference length $\bar L$ gives exactly $F=-k(L-\bar L)$, an ordinary spring. The viscous flow only moves $\bar L$, with time $\tau=\eta/\beta k$, towards a mix of the current length $L$ and the rest length $\bar L^0$ weighted by $\beta$, the fraction of force relaxed at long times. Other memory kernels change only how fast $\bar L$ moves, not where it goes.

children.title: Elastic stability, bistability and snap-through
children.body: A structure in quasi-static equilibrium sits at a stationary point of its elastic energy $E(q)$, where the generalized forces $-\partial E/\partial q$ vanish. The equilibrium is stable when it is a local minimum, which for a smooth energy means that the Hessian $\partial^2E/\partial q_a\partial q_b$ is positive definite; a maximum or a saddle is unstable. A bistable structure has two minima, like a shallow arch or a shell that can be inverted. When a slowly varied parameter, such as a load, deforms the energy so that a minimum merges with a neighbouring saddle, the lowest eigenvalue of the Hessian reaches zero and the minimum disappears. The structure then jumps dynamically to the remaining minimum, releasing stored energy: snap-through. The von Mises truss, two bars meeting at a loaded point, is the textbook example of elastic stability and snap-through. In the paper the slowly varied parameter is the set of reference lengths, moved by relaxation.

To understand the dynamics of the system, we choose the following protocol; the mass is taken from rest, where , abruptly to and held there for a finite time. That is, at the reference lengths are at the rest length values whereas the springs are held at the configuration . By Eq. 4 during the holding the reference lengths evolve along the line connecting and up to a stationary position between them (See FIG. 3). We note that due to the relaxation the reference lengths assume values not on the curve of admissible lengths, , and therefore do not correspond to any realizable configuration of the system. Nevertheless might have stable realizable configurations. An elastic equilibrium corresponds to a point of minimal “distance” according to (7) between and . Geometrically, this minimization condition is satisfied if the line between the reference lengths and the configuration is normal to the admissible lengths curve (see FIG. 3). After the release of the mass from it will elastically snap to the closest stable point. Using this geometrical interpretation of the viscoelastic quasi-static evolution, we can explain how different values of create different dynamical phases.

children.body: The Von-Mises truss SLS models displays non-trivial phenomenology of instabilities of viscoelastic systems, all of which are intuitively explained through the graphical representation. If the system at rest can be brought to another locally stable equilibrium, then the equilibrium point will remain unchanged despite the visco-elastic evolution. In particular it will never become unstable. Conversely, state that lose stability at a finite time must have not been stable with respect to their rest state and their stability must have been acquired through relaxation. Last, every acquired stable point cannot remain stable indefinitely and must become unstable. The results obtained here were obtained for the specific geometry and constitutive relations of the Von-Mises SLS system. However, they remain valid for rather general linear visco-elastic systems. In appendix we show that they hold for an arbitrary collection of SLS’s provided the mass they are connected to is constrained to move along a line and they all share the same and . We next come to generalize these result for the general isotropic and incompressible three dimensional linearly viscoelastic continua.

gist.html: Rest-stable states never destabilize; states that lose stability had acquired it, and acquired stability is eventually lost.
Holding a viscoelastic truss inverted gives three phases: never bistable, always bistable, or bistable for a while.

brief.html: In a von Mises truss of three standard linear solids, the elastic energy is the squared distance between the reference lengths and the curve of lengths the truss can take. Holding the mass inverted pulls the reference point straight towards the held lengths; stable states are where normals from it meet the curve. As the stiffness ratio $\alpha$ falls, the truss is never bistable, bistable only for a while after release, or always bistable. A stable state reached from rest never moves, and only acquired stability is lost.

gist.html: In one dimension, evolving rest lengths explain when a truss of viscoelastic springs acquires and then loses stability.

brief.html: A standard linear solid behaves at every instant like a spring of stiffness $k$, whose reference length relaxes partly towards the current length and partly back to its rest length. For a truss of three such elements, the elastic energy becomes a squared distance in a plane of lengths, so stability can be read off a drawing. Holding the truss inverted can create a second stable state that is later lost, while a stable state reached from rest never moves; an appendix extends both rules to any such assembly on a line.

children.body: We now turn to discuss linear viscoelasticity of continuous bodies. Such systems are amenable to a geometric reformulation similar to what we did for the SLS model. Here we need to exploit an infinitesimal analog of the evolving reference lengths, which we achive by resorting to an elastic description using metric tensors.

gist.html: Continuous bodies need an infinitesimal reference length: a metric tensor.

children.title: Metric tensors and strain in elasticity
children.body: Label each material point by coordinates $x^i$ that move with it. A configuration places the point at $\mathbf r(x)$ in space, and the squared distance between neighbouring points is $g_{ij}dx^idx^j$ with $g_{ij}=\partial_i\mathbf r\cdot\partial_j\mathbf r$, the metric induced by the configuration. Rigid motions leave $g_{ij}$ unchanged, so the metric records exactly the deformation. If the body would be stress-free with lengths given by a reference metric $\bar g_{ij}$, the natural strain is $\varepsilon_{ij}=\tfrac12(g_{ij}-\bar g_{ij})$, the Green–Lagrange strain, and the elastic energy density is quadratic in it, with indices raised by a metric. For an ordinary body $\bar g_{ij}$ is the metric of its relaxed shape, but it can be any metric, even one that no shape in space realizes, as in growing tissue. The paper treats a viscoelastic body in these metric tensors: at each instant elastic, about a reference metric that slowly changes.

In linear viscoelasticity the stress is a stiffness term plus a fading memory integral of the strain. Since fast deformations leave $\bar g_{ij}$ unchanged, it is the slow state variable of the material.

The quasi static evolution gives an intuitive interpretation of the slow evolution of viscoelastic bodies. Over time, the material’s configuration quickly minimizes its ’distance’ to the reference metric. The idea that in viscoelasticity bodies adapts to their configuration is implemented by the slow dynamics of the reference metric from the rest reference metric toward the recent configurations. This coupled evolution of and is also simpler to analyze both numerically and theoretically compared with the full dynamics.

Because relaxation is slow, the body always minimizes its instantaneous elastic energy about the drifting reference metric.

brief.html: A viscoelastic body has no free energy, but over short times its virtual work equals an instantaneous elastic energy about $\bar g_{ij}$. When elastic responses are much faster than relaxation, inertia drops out: the configuration minimizes this energy, with vanishing generalized forces and a positive Hessian. The motion is then a fast minimization of the distance to $\bar g_{ij}$ while $\bar g_{ij}$ slowly drifts, simpler to analyse than the full dynamics.

children.body: In section II B we describe how the evolution of the reference lengths in discrete, 1D systems can result in non trivial evolution of the configuration (characterized by ). When the parameter is appropriately set the von-Mises truss could acquire new type of stable states; namely states that are unstable initially, but acquire stability through stress relaxation at a strained state. Such states also exist for continuous viscoelastic systems, and similarly to the discrete case described above can be shown in some cases to not be able to remain stable indefinitely.

gist.html: Continua, like the truss, can acquire stable states through relaxation that cannot always last.

children.body: A given reference metric can yield multiple elastically stable configurations of the instantaneous elastic energy functional (14). Under external loading, as the reference metric slowly evolves viscoelastically according to Eq. (13) it could acquire new stable configurations, merge existing stable points or cause stable elastic configurations to lose their stability. Acquiring stability is most easily understood by examining loading at constant displacements. Consider a body taken from rest to an initially unstable configuration . The body is held fixed at this position and the reference metric starts from and slowly advances toward the metric , and the forces pushing the body away from its present state gradually relax. When releasing the body an initially unstable metrics near might display transient stability. This phenomenon is called acquired stability.

gist.html: A body held in an unstable shape may be stable when released: acquired stability.

children.body: State with acquired stability lose their stability through delayed stability loss. Seemingly stable state gradually creep until at some point elastic stability is lost, and the body rapidly snaps to a near stable configuration. Both acquired stability and delayed stability loss are expected for linear viscoelastic bodies, close to multi-stability. Described quantitatively in section IV below, as the memory kernel become comparable to the stiffness, more configurations are able to acquire stability.

gist.html: Acquired stability ends in delayed stability loss, a creep then a snap; both are expected near multistability.
Holding a continuum in an unstable shape can make it transiently stable; that acquired stability is later lost.

brief.html: As the reference metric evolves, stable configurations can appear, merge or disappear. A body held in an unstable shape relaxes towards it, and when released may stay there for a while: acquired stability. Such states creep until they suddenly snap, which is delayed stability loss. Both are expected near multistability, and more shapes can acquire stability as the memory kernel grows comparable to the stiffness.

children.body: Considering isotropic materials the stiffness and memory kernel tensors and further simplify. Isotropicity is the infinitesimal invariance to rotation in some configuration of the body. More generally, it is the infinitesimal invariance to orthogonal transformations induced by some metric on the body. This metric describes how each piece of the body should be deformed in order to have the same value under rotations.

gist.html: Isotropy is invariance under the rotations of some metric on the body, which must be specified.

children.body:
By Eq. (14), the metric associated with the stiffness is the metric used to raise the indices of the elastic strain to create the scalar energy density. In linear elasticity, in which , the stiffness is usually taken as isotropic with respect to the reference metric  Efrati et al. (2009). This amounts to assuming the body is isotropic in the undeformed configuration. The natural generalization of this assumption to viscoelasticity is to take the stiffness as isotropic with respect to the instantaneous reference metric . This will yield isotropic response properties about the instantaneous stress free state. However, an isotropic elastic response is often intimately related to isotropic material composition and internal structure which in our case is set by the rest reference metric . Therefore, we assume here the stiffness tensor to be isotropic with respect to the rest reference metric

(16)

We note that in principle, some materials may display a different constitutive behaviors, and in particular be isotropic with respect the instantaneous reference metric in which case the elasticity tensor should be adapted accordingly. Moreover, while it is reasonable to assume that the memory kernel accounting for the viscoelastic response will also be isotropic with respect to , there is no restriction preventing it from being isotropic with respect to any linear combination of and .

gist.html: The stiffness is taken isotropic about the rest metric, set by the material's composition, not the instantaneous one.

children.title: Isotropic stiffness and the Poisson ratio
children.body: An isotropic linear elastic material has only two independent elastic constants. Its stiffness tensor can be written $C^{ijkl}=\lambda h^{ij}h^{kl}+2\mu h^{ik}h^{jl}$, where $h$ is the metric that defines rotations and $\lambda,\mu$ are the Lamé constants, $\mu$ being the shear modulus. The energy density $\tfrac12C^{ijkl}\varepsilon_{ij}\varepsilon_{kl}$ is then $\tfrac\lambda2(\operatorname{tr}\varepsilon)^2+\mu\operatorname{tr}\varepsilon^2$: one term penalizes changes of volume, the other changes of shape. An equivalent pair is Young's modulus $E$ and the Poisson ratio $\nu=\lambda/2(\lambda+\mu)$, the ratio of lateral contraction to axial extension of a stretched bar. As $\lambda/\mu\to\infty$, volume changes become infinitely costly, $\nu\to1/2$, and the material is incompressible; rubbers come close to this. For isotropic stiffness the paper's choice is which metric plays the role of $h$: it takes the rest reference metric.

The assumption of homogeneity is usually obtained by taking the tensor at hand as constant in space. However, because both and are densities of properties, homogeneity is a matter of measure. Directly from Eq. (14), constant stiffness gives equal energy density per ’initial’ volume element (with the same deformation). Here too, in principle, one can account for other measures induced by other metrics, and thus for different types of homogeneity. Thus even when a material is considered isotropic and homogeneous, there are some choices as to how to express these symmetries in the constitutive relations.

gist.html: Homogeneity is a matter of measure: constant stiffness means equal energy per initial volume.

brief.html: At stationarity the generalized forces are $(1-\beta)$ times those of the rest system, so stationary configurations are its extremals. The stationary Hessian is $(1-\beta)$ times the rest Hessian plus a positive term, so rest-stable shapes are stationary and rest saddles may stabilize for good. Brought suddenly from rest into a stable shape, a body never moves: its reference metric slides along the line towards it, and the elastic strain shrinks by a common factor. The proofs need a scalar kernel, which incompressibility provides.

children.body: We have so far discussed the behavior of viscoelastic systems in states that are stable when arrived to from rest. We next come to discuss the complementary states that are unstable. In particular we would like to address how could they acquire stability and also in turn how this stability is lost. Jumping poppers are thin rubber shells. Very thin poppers display almost isometric bi-stability, while thick poppers have only one elastically stable shape. However, when an appropriately cut popper is flipped inside out and laid on the table [Fig. (5)] it creeps for a few seconds and snaps back to its original shape, much in the same manner systems with intermediate values of in the Von-Mises truss model of section II B acquired and lost stability.

gist.html: An inverted, suitably cut jumping popper creeps for seconds then snaps back, like the intermediate-stiffness truss.

children.body: One general corollary of the previous section is that stability loss can occur only from configurations that were “originally” unstable - not a stable configuration of the rest elastic system . If the configuration was originally stable, than by the above claim it is also stationary, and its stability can never be lost. Thus a system exhibiting temporary stability followed by a snap though, was necessarily away of its rest system before the free evolution. Therefore if a popper snap a finite time after being inverted, its stability (prior to the snap) was necessarily acquired, presumably by holding it inverted for a long enough duration.

gist.html: Stability can be lost only if it was acquired, so a popper that snaps late had been relaxed while inverted.

children.body: Second, acquired stability from configurations that were not extremal initially (e.g. saddle points) cannot persist indefinitely and must be eventually lost. If a configuration is stationary after a relaxation that started from rest then it must also be extremal with respect to the rest reference metric. In the case of the popper it means that if it was originally unstable, there is no way (by holdings the popper inverted or by any other deformations) to stabilize the popper indefinitely after the external loads are removed. For such cases the inverted shapes cannot be stationary states of the system, and the popper will always eventually snap back to an rest state.

gist.html: Acquired stability of a configuration that is not a rest extremal must end: such a popper always snaps back.

brief.html: Jumping poppers, thin rubber shells, can creep for seconds after being turned inside out and then snap back, like the truss at intermediate stiffness. Since rest-stable shapes are stationary, a shape that loses stability was unstable at rest and had acquired its stability, presumably while held. A stationary shape must be a rest extremal, so an inverted popper that was unstable at rest cannot be stabilized indefinitely and always snaps back. A simulated cone gives the flip time against thickness.

gist.html: For incompressible solids, stable shapes reached from rest never evolve, and only acquired stability can be lost.

brief.html: For incompressible materials the memory kernel is scalar, so the reference metric relaxes towards $\bar g^{\rm stat}_{ij}=\beta g_{ij}+(1-\beta)\bar g^0_{ij}$. Every stationary configuration is therefore an equilibrium of the body at its rest metric, and every configuration stable there is stationary. A body brought suddenly from rest into such a stable shape never moves, whatever the memory kernel. Hence only stability acquired by relaxation can be lost, and acquired stability of shapes that are not rest equilibria must be lost, as for jumping poppers.

children.body: Naively one expects stress relaxation to only diminish internal forces and thus act to stabilize a system rendering the notion of viscoelastic instabilities elusive. We have shown this intuition to indeed be correct; if a system is brought abruptly from its rest state into an elastically meta-stable state then stress relaxation will never cause it to lose stability. We moreover proved that in such a setting the configuration of the system will show no evolution despite the continuous vicoelastic attenuation of internal stresses.

gist.html: The naive intuition holds: a metastable state reached abruptly from rest never loses stability or moves.

children.body: Having formulated the viscoelastic evolution in terms of metric tensors we observed that the instantaneous reference metric evolves not only toward , the assumed configuration, but also toward , its rest metric. When starting from rest only the former is observed. In this case the reference metric evolves along a straight line and as a result the elastic energy minimizer at time with respect to remains the minimizer for subsequent times, as explained graphically in FIG. (4). For every other case, in which does not evolve solely toward , we expect a visible creep and in particular such systems may display viscoelastic instabilities. We have shown that the only states that can display viscoelastic instabilities are states that are elastically unstable with respect to but have acquired stability through stress relaxation. We have also shown that every instance of such an acquired stability cannot persist indefinitely and must be lost in time.

gist.html: Only states unstable about the rest metric that acquired stability can snap, and that acquired stability cannot last.

children.body: These results are expected to hold for every isotropic and incompressible linearly viscoelastic material regardless of the form of history dependence of the stress relaxation kernel. However, considering a single SLS system or any other purely one dimensional viscoelastic system we do not observe this rich phenomenology of instabilities due to the trivial structure of the set of admissible states. The ability of a viscoelastic system to display delayed instabilities relies on the non-trivial shape of the set of admissible states. As observed in FIG. (3) for the SLS Von-Misses truss, only when the set of admissible states is sufficiently curved can it support multi-stability. For continuous media the structure of admissible (Euclidean) states is non-convex. As a result we may bring a systems that is initially at rest in an Euclidean configuration, to another Euclidean state by the application of external forces, and the viscoelastic evolution will result in a non-Euclidean instantaneous reference metric, giving rise to a geometrically frustrated state. In such cases residual stress is like to appear even in lieu of multistability.

gist.html: Delayed instabilities need a curved set of admissible states; in continua relaxation can also leave residual stress.

children.title: Non-Euclidean reference metrics and residual stress
children.body: Not every metric is the metric of some shape in space. A metric on a three-dimensional body comes from a configuration $\mathbf r(x)$ only if it is Euclidean, which means that its Riemann curvature tensor vanishes everywhere; these are the compatibility conditions of elasticity. A reference metric with curvature, called non-Euclidean or incompatible, cannot be realized: whatever shape the body takes, some pieces are stretched or compressed relative to their preferred lengths. The body then carries residual stress even with no external load, and is said to be geometrically frustrated. Such states arise in growing leaves and tissues, in swelling gels, and under non-uniform heating, and are the subject of non-Euclidean (incompatible) elasticity. The set of Euclidean metrics is not convex, so a mixture of two of them is generally non-Euclidean; this is why a reference metric relaxing between a rest metric and a held one can leave a frustrated state.

While in the theory presented here the rest metric, , is assumed constant one could consider growing tissue or plastically deforming material by allowing the rest metric to vary in time. The variation could be provided by external conditions or obey some additional constitutive relations. This will result in a covariant elaso-visco-plastic theory. Such a description may provide crucial insight into growing and deforming biological polymers where a rapid growth or shrinkage events may be masked by the slow evolution of the instantaneous reference metric. The applicability of such a theory, reminiscent of the additive decomposition of strains Lee (1969); Efrati et al. (2013), to growing and deforming tissue remains to shown.

gist.html: Letting the rest metric evolve could give a covariant theory of growth and plasticity, not yet tested.
Relaxation does stabilize states reached from rest; instabilities need acquired stability and a curved set of admissible shapes.

brief.html: The naive intuition is right for states reached abruptly from rest: relaxation neither destabilizes nor moves them. When the reference metric does not evolve only towards the current shape, the body creeps and may turn unstable. Only acquired stability can be lost, and it must be unless the shape is a rest extremal. They also need a curved set of admissible states, which a single spring lacks; in continua relaxation can leave residual stress. An evolving rest metric could describe growth or plasticity, which remains to be shown.

gist.html:
• Context Rubbery solids can creep, then snap, though relaxation should only stabilize them.
  • Result
    • Viscoelasticity becomes elasticity about a reference metric drifting from rest towards recent shapes.
    • In incompressible isotropic solids, a stable shape reached suddenly from rest never moves or destabilizes.
    • In incompressible isotropic solids only acquired stability can be lost, and it always is unless the shape is a rest equilibrium.
    • A spring–dashpot truss illustrates the rules: bistability absent, lasting, or acquired then lost.
    • Rubber “jumping poppers” that snap back late had acquired their inverted stability.
  • Why it matters Rules expected to hold for any memory kernel give insight into stability over time, where simulations were relied on.

specialist.html:
• Context Linear relaxation lowers stresses, so should never destabilize a metastable state; yet viscoelastic solids creep, then snap.
  • Result
    • Viscoelasticity becomes elasticity about a reference metric $\bar g_{ij}(t)$, untouched by fast deformations, relaxing from the rest metric $\bar g^0_{ij}$ towards past configurations.
    • For isotropic incompressible media, a rest-stable configuration imposed abruptly from rest stays static and stable for any scalar kernel, its elastic strain shrinking by $1-\beta+\beta\phi(t)$.
    • As $\bar g^{\rm stat}=\beta g+(1-\beta)\bar g^0$, stationary configurations are rest extremals: only acquired stability can be lost, and non-extremals lose it, while rest saddles may stabilize permanently.
    • A three-SLS von Mises truss illustrates the rules in three phases, proved for any mass on a line tied by equally relaxing SLS elements.
    • Jumping poppers that snap late had acquired their stability; inverted non-extremal shapes cannot be kept.
  • Why it matters Rules expected to hold for any memory kernel give insight where simulations were relied on, elucidating subtle viscoelastic instabilities.

student.html:
• Context Rubbery materials can creep slowly, then snap, though relaxing stresses should only stabilize them.
  • Result
    • A viscoelastic solid acts as an elastic one whose preferred lengths drift towards recent shapes.
    • Pushed quickly from rest into another stable shape, an incompressible solid stays put.
    • Only stability created by relaxation can be lost, and a shape not balanced at rest always loses it.
    • In a spring–dashpot truss, relaxation leaves one stable state, keeps two, or briefly adds one.
    • “Jumping poppers” that snap back late had gained their inverted stability by relaxing.
  • Why it matters Simple rules, not simulations alone, may tell when rubber-like structures snap over time.

brief.html:
Rubber-like solids relax stress and creep, yet keep part of their stress indefinitely. Some creep slowly and then snap, as jumping poppers, rubber shells turned inside out, do: delayed stability loss. Laws tying stress to the whole strain history through a memory kernel simulate this well but explain little, and relaxation, which lowers stresses, seems bound to stabilize. The paper finds that intuition right for states reached abruptly from rest, and traces viscoelastic instabilities to stability that relaxation itself created.

A standard linear solid, a spring in parallel with a spring and a dashpot in series, acts at every instant as one spring, $F=-k(L-\bar L)$, about a reference length $\bar L$. Viscous flow moves $\bar L$ towards both the current length and the rest length $\bar L^0$, weighted by $\beta$, the fraction of force relaxed at long times. For a continuum the stress is likewise elastic in the difference between the actual metric $g_{ij}$ and a reference metric $\bar g_{ij}(t)$. Fast deformations leave $\bar g_{ij}$ unchanged, so it is the slow state variable, drifting from the rest metric $\bar g^0_{ij}$ towards recent shapes. Because elasticity is fast, the body always takes the admissible shape closest to $\bar g_{ij}$ in elastic energy.

In a von Mises truss of three such elements, the energy is the squared distance from the reference point to the curve of lengths the truss can take. Stable states are therefore feet of normals to that curve. Held inverted, the truss is never bistable when its symmetry-breaking spring is stiff, and always bistable when it is soft. In between, relaxation creates an inverted stable state that is lost some time after release: a delayed instability. An appendix proves the rules for any such assembly on a line sharing $\beta$ and the relaxation time.

For isotropic incompressible solids the reference metric relaxes towards $\bar g^{\rm stat}_{ij}=\beta g_{ij}+(1-\beta)\bar g^0_{ij}$, whatever the memory kernel. So stationary forces are $(1-\beta)$ times those of the rest elastic system: every stationary configuration is an equilibrium of the body at rest, and relaxation adds a positive term to its stiffness. A body brought suddenly from rest into a stable shape therefore never moves or loses stability, because its reference metric slides straight towards that shape. Only acquired stability can be lost, and stability acquired away from rest equilibria always is. A popper that snaps late had acquired its stability, and one unstable at rest cannot be kept inverted indefinitely.

The proofs need a scalar memory kernel, so they hold exactly for incompressible solids and approximately near incompressibility. Instabilities also need a curved set of admissible shapes, which a single element lacks; in continua relaxation can instead leave a non-Euclidean reference metric and residual stress. For poppers the text applies the rules qualitatively and gives simulated flip times; the comparison with experiments that the abstract mentions is not shown here. A rest metric that itself evolves, for growth or plasticity, is left open.

defs.html: A solid made of long polymer chains cross-linked into a network, such as latex or silicone rubber, or the proteins elastin and resilin in tissues. Elastomers are soft, stretch reversibly beyond 100% strain, and are viscoelastic: they creep and relax stress, yet keep their shape's topology.

The gradual drop of the force a body supports while held at a fixed deformation. In elastomeric solids it is only fractional: a finite part of the stress remains however long one waits. The paper's $\beta$ is the fraction that relaxes.

The slow, continuing deformation of a body under a constant load, the counterpart of stress relaxation at fixed deformation. In elastomers it is dissipative yet reversible. In delayed stability loss, a slow creep precedes a sudden snap.

A fast elastic instability, such as a snap, that follows a period of slow creep, so that a seemingly stable state gives way only after a delay. Examples are the Venus fly-trap, jumping poppers and, outside elastomers, some earthquakes. The paper also calls it delayed instability.

defs.html: A sudden jump of an elastic structure, typically a shell or an arch, from one shape to another, when the shape it holds stops being a minimum of its elastic energy. The stored elastic energy is released quickly.

at.quote: passive snap through of thin elastomeric shells

defs.html: A thin rubber shell that can be turned inside out. Very thin poppers are nearly isometrically bistable and stay inverted; thick ones have a single stable shape; suitably cut ones creep for a few seconds after inversion and then snap back.

In linear viscoelasticity, the function that weights past strains in the present stress, through an integral over the strain history. It fades with time, so recent history matters most. In the paper its long-time weight $\beta$ dominates questions of stability; its form only influences the timing.

The length at which a spring exerts no force. The paper uses it in two senses: in the introduction for the evolving length of a viscoelastic element (in the body its reference length $\bar L$), and in the body for the fixed length $\bar L^0$ the element would reach if left free indefinitely.

The simplest spring–dashpot model with both a finite instantaneous stiffness and only partial stress relaxation: a spring $(1-\beta)k$ in parallel with a spring $\beta k$ and a dashpot of viscosity $\eta$ in series. Abbreviated SLS; its relaxation time is $\tau=\eta/\beta k$.

A classic model of snap-through: a point held by two inclined bars, with two mirror-image stable positions. Here the bars are standard linear solids, the point is a mass moving along a line, and a third, vertical element of relative stiffness $\alpha$ breaks the symmetry.

at.quote: in the form of a Von-Misses truss

defs.html: Stability that holds only for a time: a configuration is a local minimum of the elastic energy about the present reference lengths or metric, but stops being one as these keep relaxing. The truss at intermediate stiffness and a released inverted popper show it.

at.quote: first example of transient elastic stability

defs.html: A state that no longer changes in time. The paper uses it in two senses: for the truss, a configuration that stays fixed while its reference lengths still relax; for continua and in the appendix, a state in which both the configuration and the reference metric have stopped.

at.quote: stability and stationarity of a general 1D

defs.html: For one viscoelastic element, the length $\bar L$ about which it acts as an ordinary spring, $F=-k(L-\bar L)$. It combines the springs' rest lengths and the dashpot's extension, so fast stretching leaves it unchanged, while viscous flow moves it towards the current length and the rest length $\bar L^0$.

The elastic energy computed about the present reference lengths or metric, held fixed. A dissipative body has no true free energy, but over short times this one governs its response; for a continuum it is quadratic in the elastic strain $\tfrac12(g_{ij}-\bar g_{ij})$.

The lengths that the truss's springs can actually take together as the mass moves, $(L_1(z),\alpha L_2(z))$: a curve in the plane of normalized lengths. Reference lengths can lie anywhere in the plane, and the elastic energy is the squared distance from them to a point of the curve.

at.quote: a point on the admissible lengths

defs.html: The metric about which a viscoelastic body is, at each instant, simply elastic: the stress is the stiffness times half of $g_{ij}-\bar g_{ij}$. Fast deformations leave it unchanged; it relaxes slowly from the rest reference metric towards recent configurations. It is the continuum analogue of the reference length.

at.quote: time dependent three dimensional reference metric

defs.html: The paper's formulation of viscoelasticity: a body is described by its actual metric, the lengths it has, and by an evolving reference metric, the lengths it would locally like to have, with the stress elastic in their difference. It is covariant: written in material coordinates, valid for any choice of them.

Treating the motion as a sequence of elastic equilibria. Elastic responses are much faster than viscoelastic relaxation, so inertia is dropped and the configuration at each moment minimizes the instantaneous elastic energy about the current reference lengths or metric.

The paper's word for isotropy: invariance of the material response under rotations. In a body described by metrics, rotations are defined only relative to some metric, so one must say which; the paper takes stiffness and memory kernel isotropic with respect to the rest reference metric.

Keeping its volume under deformation (Poisson ratio $\nu=1/2$). The paper assumes the incompressible contraction also holds during relaxation, which makes the metric memory kernel scalar; its continuum stability claims are proved under this assumption and hold approximately near it.

The metric $g_{ij}=\partial_i\mathbf r\cdot\partial_j\mathbf r$ that a configuration $\mathbf r$ of the body in space induces on its material coordinates. It gives the actual distances between neighbouring material points, and fixes the configuration up to rigid motions.

The metric on which the body is locally stress-free and stationary: the lengths each small piece would reach if cut out and left to relax indefinitely. It encodes the material's structure, is constant in time in this paper, and plays the role of the rest length $\bar L^0$.

defs.html: A measure of stress referred to the undeformed body rather than the deformed one: contracted with a change of strain it gives the work done per unit reference volume. Here it is the work conjugate of the metric, per volume $\sqrt{\bar g^0}\,d^3x$.

The memory kernel rewritten for the reference metric, the inverse stiffness times the stress kernel: it says how past metrics feed the present reference metric. For isotropic materials it has a scalar part $\beta\phi(s)$ and a part $\psi(s)$ mixing components; incompressibility removes the latter.

A configuration at which the energy is stationary, so all generalized forces vanish: a minimum, a maximum or a saddle. The paper calls a configuration stable only when it is a minimum, with positive definite Hessian, so an extremal need not be stable.

defs.html: Stability gained through stress relaxation: a configuration unstable about the rest state becomes, after the body is held in or near it, a local minimum of the instantaneous elastic energy, so it persists when released. Such states later creep and may snap, in delayed stability loss.

at.quote: This phenomenon is called acquired stability

defs.html: Uniformity of the material's properties across the body. Since stiffness and memory kernel are densities, the paper notes that uniform depends on the volume used; it takes them constant per initial volume $\sqrt{\bar g^0}\,d^3x$, so equal deformations of equal rest volumes cost equal energy.

The purely elastic body whose reference metric (or reference lengths) equals the rest one, $\bar g_{ij}=\bar g^0_{ij}$: the material with all relaxation undone. “Originally stable” means stable in this system; the paper shows that stationary viscoelastic configurations are its extremals.

defs.html: A stability postulate of continuum mechanics, here in the form that the stiffness tensor is positive definite, so any non-zero strain costs elastic energy. The paper uses it to show that relaxation adds a positive definite term to the Hessian of the stationary energy.

Said of a body whose reference metric is non-Euclidean, so that no shape in space realizes all its preferred lengths at once and stress remains in every configuration: residual stress. The paper notes that viscoelastic relaxation can produce such a state from a Euclidean start.

questions.q: What do $\beta$, $\tau$, $\alpha$, the bars and the zeros mean?
questions.a: $\beta$, between 0 and 1, is the fraction of force or stress relaxed after a long hold at fixed deformation: 0 is elastic, 1 a Maxwell fluid. $\tau=\eta/\beta k$ is the relaxation time. A bar marks a reference quantity, $\bar L$ or $\bar g_{ij}(t)$, which evolves; a zero marks a rest quantity, $\bar L^0$ or $\bar g^0_{ij}$, which is fixed; $g_{ij}$ is the actual metric. $\alpha$ is the truss stiffness ratio $\sqrt{k_2/2k_1}$, but also labels generalized coordinates $\lambda_\alpha$ and a mixing term $\alpha(x,t)$.

questions.q: Is the reference length a new physical assumption?
questions.a: No. For the standard linear solid it is an exact regrouping of the springs' rest lengths and the dashpot's length, and the paper calls its equations a mere reformulation of familiar viscoelastic dynamics. What it adds is a variable that fast deformations leave unchanged, so the element is an ordinary spring at every instant, and stability questions become geometric questions about where the reference lengths have moved.

questions.q: Why must the truss at intermediate stiffness snap back, rather than settle in its acquired state?
questions.a: After release the reference point keeps moving, towards a stationary mix of the current lengths and the rest lengths. A stationary state would have to be an equilibrium of the truss at its rest lengths, and at this stiffness the only stable one is the original position. So the inverted state cannot become stationary, its stability is lost at some time, and the truss snaps back.

questions.q: Why does only $\beta$, and not the shape of the memory kernel, decide stability?
questions.a: With a scalar kernel the reference metric relaxes towards $\bar g^{\rm stat}=\beta g+(1-\beta)\bar g^0$ whatever the kernel's shape; the kernel sets only how fast it gets there. Stationary states and their stability depend on that endpoint, hence on $\beta$ alone, while the kernel affects the time it takes to reach an instability. That is why the exponential kernel of the standard linear solid suffices.

questions.q: Why does a stable shape reached abruptly from rest not creep at all, although its stresses relax?
questions.a: Starting from rest, the reference metric moves along the straight line from the rest metric towards the held configuration metric, so the elastic strain only shrinks by a common factor $1-\beta+\beta\phi(t)$. Forces that vanished at the start keep vanishing, and the Hessian stays a mix of the initial positive one and a positive stiffness term. The configuration therefore remains the closest admissible one throughout.

questions.q: Can relaxation permanently stabilize a shape that was unstable at rest?
questions.a: Only if it is an extremal of the rest system, such as a saddle point. The stationary Hessian is $(1-\beta)$ times the rest one plus a positive term, so a saddle can become stable indefinitely, the more easily the closer $\beta$ is to 1. A shape that is not a rest extremal cannot be stationary, so any stability it acquires must eventually be lost.

questions.q: Why do the continuum claims need incompressibility?
questions.a: The proofs use a scalar metric memory kernel, so that relaxation moves every component of the reference metric towards the same mix of current and rest metrics. A compressible isotropic material has a second kernel $\psi$, which mixes components through changes of volume and breaks this collinearity. The paper states that the results still hold approximately, deviating less the closer the material is to incompressible; it does not estimate the deviation.

questions.q: Isotropic with respect to which metric, and does the choice matter?
questions.a: Rotations of a body described by metrics are defined only by a chosen metric. The paper takes the stiffness and memory kernel isotropic with respect to the rest reference metric, because isotropy reflects the material's composition, which the rest metric encodes. A material isotropic about the instantaneous reference metric is possible in principle and would need a different stiffness tensor; the paper does not treat it.

questions.q: Must a popper be held inverted for it to snap back late?
questions.a: The argument fixes only that a popper which snaps a finite time after inversion had acquired its stability, since a shape stable at rest and reached from rest never loses it. How it was acquired is left open: holding it inverted long enough is the presumable route. Conversely, if the inverted shape was unstable at rest, no holding or other deformation keeps it inverted for good.

questions.q: Does the paper compare its predictions with experiments on poppers?
questions.a: Not in this text. The abstract mentions quantitative agreement with experiments on silicone rubber shells, but the popper section applies the stability rules qualitatively, and its figure shows a simulated cone ($\beta=0.3$, $\nu=0.47$) with flip times against thickness, noting a similar phase plot in earlier work and in a companion paper by the same authors. Measured data and a direct comparison are not shown here.

questions.q: Why does a single viscoelastic element show none of these instabilities?
questions.a: A single element, or any purely one-dimensional system, has a trivial set of admissible states, so its elastic energy has a single minimum about any reference length. Multistability, and with it acquired and lost stability, needs a sufficiently curved set of admissible states, as in the truss. In continua the Euclidean metrics form a non-convex set, which supplies the curvature and can also leave residual stress.

questions.q: Could the rest metric itself change, as in growth or plasticity?
questions.a: In this theory it is constant. The paper suggests that letting it evolve, driven externally or by further constitutive relations, would give a covariant elasto-visco-plastic theory for growing tissue or plastic flow, in which fast growth could be masked by the slow relaxation of the reference metric. It does not develop this, and says its applicability remains to be shown.
